searchText: IIUC, you are proposing the following? ``` rlp([Type0, Payload0, Type1, Payload1, ..., TypeN, PayloadN]) ``` Yes, that’s it I'm not personally a fan. Heterogeneous lists are more complex to process than homogeneous lists, and the type and the payloads are tightly coupled tuples which I dislike splitting (again, because it slightly complicates processing). In both cases, the lists are heterogeneous ~~I don't believe this is true?~~ Ah, it depends on how you handle legacy internally. 1) we have tx items and byte arrays 2) we have tx items, type bytes If you treat legacy transactions as typed transactions with types `0xf8-0xfa` then it is heterogeneous. I’m not sure how they can be homogeneous? Unless you wrap legacy txs in a byte array? At the list chunking stage of processing, treat them all as Typed Transactions. Which means switch on the first byte, dispatch to appropriate transaction processor based on that byte. But that means we’d have to wrap legacy txs in byte arrays? If we wanted them homogeneous, I think the only ways is to byte array wrap each tx - otherwise txs with types will always be different. Switching on the length byte of legacy txs is different than a type byte because after the type byte is the length prefix of the payload. No, you can just treat the first byte of legacy transactions as a type byte. There are only 3 possible (in reality) leading bytes. So there would be 3 legacy transaction types in this model. But that is different than a typed tx - the typed tx goes `type || payload len || payload` and the legacy tx goes `type (also length) || payload` Correct. It really depends on how you architect things internally. ```py for (transactionBytes in transactionList): switch (transactionBytes[0]): case 1: process2930(transactionBytes.slice(1)) break case 0xf8: case 0xf9: case 0xfa: processLegacy(transactionBytes) break default: throw ``` There are some other designs of course, that is just one that is made possible and is nice and simple if you have a homogeneous list. ```py type = txBytes[0] payload = txBytes.slice(1) switch (type) case 1: process2930(payload) case 0xf8: case 0xf9: case 0xfa: processLegacy([type, ...payload]) ``` is another similar and possible design. Back to the original point though, to get to the two designs you’ve shown, we’d need to first parse out those bytes of an RLP byte array It’s more optimal to not do that. I’m not sure if there is a downside I’m missing to approach 2? Hmm, why is it optimal to not parse the RLP array? I believe have to parse the full array to check the bounds, then parse to get out the actual tx ```py txList = rlp_decode(messageBytes) for (txBytes in txList): type = txBytes[0] payload = txBytes.slice(1) switch (type): case 1: process2930(payload) break case 0xf8: case 0xf9: case 0xfa: processLegacy([type, ...payload]) break ``` Hmm, can you type up some pseudocode to show what you mean? I don't think I'm following. Ah, you are using a streaming RLP decoder perhaps? Yes it’s a streaming decoder You *should* still be able to stream process I think? In your example, it seems like you’re assuming that every txs is a byte array, but 2718 only defines typed txs to be a byte array - legacy are RLP elements The first bytes of an RLP list item are its length IIRC. It is a byte array from the perspective of the outer RLP list. A byte array is prefixed by b8-bf, this is slightly different than an RLP element ``` rlp([ rlp([nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data, v, r, s]), 1 || rlp([chainId, nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data, access_list, yParity, r, s]) ..., ]) ``` Both of those list items are byte arrays according to the outer `rlp` list. So really it is the following in terms of rlp types: ``` rlp([bytes, bytes]) ``` Hmm, though perhaps people don't realize this and don't agree with it. ```py for (el in rlpStream): switch el.type(): case rlp.List: processLegacy(el) break case rlp.String: payload = el.toString() type = payload[0] process2718(type, payload) break ``` this is what it would currently look like from my perspective Maybe everyone is assuming that legacy transactions are just lists in the outer array... that's what i've been assuming That isn't how the spec is written, but I am worried now that other people have the same misunderstanding as you do. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2976 is explicit on this subject, but I can see how it would be easy to overlook. so 2718 is supposed to wrap all txs in an RLP byte array? 2718 doesn't. 2976 does. 2718 doesn't define how transactions are gossiped. 2718 only defines how they are prepared for merklization. ah okay, there are no lists of transaction in the consensus mechanism ```py TransactionPayload = Bytes # dependent on TransactionType LegacyTransaction = Bytes # rlp([...]) Transaction = (TransactionType | TransactionPayload) || LegacyTransaction transactionRoot = patriciaTrie(rlp(Index) => Transaction) ``` hmm 2976 says that legacy txs are an RLP encoded array of the form [nonce, ...] - this would be different then saying they are the rlpByteArray(rlp(tx)), no? The return type of `rlp_encode(x)` is a byte array. yes, but that array starts with `f8|f9|fa` were an RLP byte array starts with `b8|...|bf` ``` rlp([rlp([...])]) != rlp([[...]]) ``` This isn't SSZ. 😉 i guess i'm confused - if i want to encode raw opaque bytes in RLP, that is an RLP byte array starting with `b8|...|bf` no? According to 2976 as currently written, a legacy transaction is RLP encoded, which returns a byte array (we can ignore what bytes are in that array for now). That byte array is then an item in the transaction list which is then RLP encoded. ```py transaction1 = rlp_encode([nonce1, ...]) transaction2 = rlp_encode([nonce2, ...]) transaction3 = Bytes.concat(1, rlp_encode([chainId3, ...])) transaction4 = Bytes.concat(1, rlp_encode([chainId4, ...])) transactionList = rlp_encode([transaction1, transaction2, transaction3, transaction4]) ``` I'm talking about the RLP type "byte array" not the bytes that represent some RLP structure To make sure we are on the same page, this is the type of the parameter to `rlp_encode` and the type of the return value of `rlp_decode`: ```ts // | is the union operator type RlpItem = ByteArray | RlpItem[] ``` okay got it, RlpItem is either a byte array or a list of other rlp items In the case of the `transactionList` for devp2p, it is an RLP encoded array of ByteArrays. excerpts.content:
The outer transaction list is a list of rlp items, which means it starts with `f8-ff` (almost always `f8` though in our case).  Every item in this particular list is a byte array, so it is length prefixed with something between `00-bf`.  In our case this will always be more than 55 bytes so we'll need length bytes which means `b8-bf` (pragmatically, always `b8 or b9` in our case) followed by one or two length bytes and then the bytes themselves.

Those bytes are themselves an RLP encoded list in the case of legacy transactions, or it will be a `concat(type, payload)` for a 2718 transaction.  In your example it is a single legacy transaction, which means the first byte is going to be `f8-fa`.  If it was 2930, it would start with `1`.
